extracted.intended_audience: general readers, media students, broadcasters and television industry professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Overview guidance and definitional standards for television systems, formats, programming distribution, funding/advertising models, genre/cost considerations, broadcast regulation, and social/environmental impacts relevant to producing or evaluating television content and services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard-definition television (SDTV) resolution definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard-definition television or SDTV refers to two different resolutions: 576i, with 576 interlaced lines of resolution, derived from the European-developed PAL and SECAM systems, and 480i based on the American National Television System Committee NTSC system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SDTV uses a resolution not considered HDTV (720p, 1080i, 1080p, 1440p, 4K UHDTV, and 8K UHD) or enhanced-definition television (EDTV 480p). In North America, digital SDTV is broadcast in the same 4:3 aspect ratio as NTSC signals (widescreen content being center cut); in PAL/SECAM countries SDTV is usually shown with a 16:9 aspect ratio, with older 4:3 programs shown as 4:3 or pillarboxed/ anamorphically scaled as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-definition television (HDTV) format standards
rubrics_metrics.description: High-definition television (HDTV) provides a resolution that is substantially higher than that of standard-definition television. HDTV may be transmitted in various formats: 1080p (1920×1080p), 1080i (1920×1080i), 720p (1280×720p), and non-standard CEA resolutions such as 1440×1080i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pixel counts per frame/field are provided (e.g., 1080p ~2,073,600 pixels per frame; 1080i ~1,036,800 pixels per field). Use of these formats distinguishes HDTV from SDTV in broadcasting and display specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultra-high-definition television (UHD) definition and minimum requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Ultra-high-definition television includes 4K UHD (2160p) and 8K UHD (4320p). The Consumer Electronics Association defined 'Ultra High Definition' for displays that have an aspect ratio of at least 16:9 and at least one digital input capable of carrying and presenting natural video at a minimum resolution of 3840×2160 pixels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UHD naming variants (Super Hi‑Vision, Ultra HD, UltraHD, UHDTV) and theITU/industry proposals/approvals are relevant when specifying displays, inputs, and marketed capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original run (first run) versus broadcast syndication
rubrics_metrics.description: Original run or First run: a producer creates a program and shows it on a station or network that has paid for or licensed the production. Broadcast syndication: secondary programming usages beyond the original run, including secondary domestic runs and international usage, often managed/sold by other companies or stations under contract from copyright holders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syndication involves selling the product into markets allowed by contract; management may be delegated to other companies. The distinction affects licensing, rights, revenue streams, and distribution strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programming distribution practices and territorial differences
rubrics_metrics.description: First-run programming is increasing on subscription services outside the United States, but few domestically produced programs are syndicated on domestic free-to-air (FTA) elsewhere; repeat FTA screenings usually only occur on the originating network, and affiliates rarely buy non-network programming not focused on local programming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These distribution norms affect decisions about producing content for international sale versus local broadcast, and influence syndication strategies and expectations by territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television genre classification and production-cost implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Television genres include a broad range; the most expensive entertainment genres to produce are usually dramas, while the least expensive are game shows, talk shows, variety shows, and reality television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genre choice has cost implications (e.g., historical Westerns may be costly). Genres overlap (sci‑fi may be drama or action). Use archetypal examples (sitcoms, animated adult series, game shows) when planning budgets and scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of 'quality television' (fictional and nonfictional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictional series argued to be 'quality television' exhibit traits also found in art films, such as psychological realism, narrative complexity, and ambiguous plotlines. Nonfiction 'quality' includes news broadcasting and serious, noncommercial programming aimed at a niche audience, such as documentaries and public affairs shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These qualitative traits are cited by scholars and advocacy groups when evaluating a program’s cultural/critical value versus mass-entertainment metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television funding models
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast television is financed by government, advertising, licensing (a form of tax), subscription, or combinations of these sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding model determines obligations and constraints (e.g., encryption for subscription channels, restrictions on advertising for public broadcasters), revenue mix (typical global split cited: 45–50% advertising, 40–45% subscription, ~10% public funding), and strategic choices about content and access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription channel encryption and funding interplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Some TV channels are partly funded from subscriptions; therefore, the signals are encrypted during the broadcast to ensure only paying subscribers have access to decryption codes. Most subscription services are also funded by advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encryption and dual funding (subscription + advertising) affect technical requirements, rights management, and monetization approaches for channels and services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television licence/tax-funded public broadcasting model
rubrics_metrics.description: Television services in some countries may be funded by a television licence or a form of taxation, reducing or eliminating advertising. Example: the BBC’s TV service carries no advertising on UK channels and is funded by an annual television licence paid by premises receiving live telecasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licence fees are set by government though the broadcaster may claim editorial independence; different countries have variations (e.g., NHK in Japan reception fee, French 'redevance audiovisuelle'). Fee levels, exemptions/discounts, and allocation determine public broadcaster funding and programming constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television advertising formats, lengths, and placement economics
rubrics_metrics.description: Television advertisements range from brief spots (a few seconds) to several minutes and include program-length infomercials; infomercials commonly run 30 minutes or one hour. Advertising placement and rates are determined primarily by viewership metrics (e.g., Nielsen ratings), time of day, and popularity of the channel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example costs (Super Bowl, American Idol) and daypart pricing illustrate how audience measurement drives ad revenues. Product placement is another advertising form, sometimes involving low-cost provision of goods in exchange for on-screen exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory limits on advertising (United Kingdom example)
rubrics_metrics.description: UK restrictions: the big three national commercial TV channels (ITV, Channel 4, Channel 5) can show an average of only seven minutes of advertising per hour (eight minutes in peak); other broadcasters average no more than nine minutes (twelve in peak). Advertisements must not be inserted in certain proscribed program types under half an hour (news/current affairs, documentaries, children’s programs); adverts may not be carried in programs designed for schools, religious broadcasting, or during a formal Royal ceremony. There must be clear demarcations in time between programs and advertisements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules shape scheduling, program editing (removal of US-style ad breaks), and compliance responsibilities; broadcasters must plan content and ad breaks to satisfy legal/regulatory constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast programming scheduling and automation
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast programming is the practice of organizing television programs in a schedule, with broadcast automation used to regularly change scheduling to build an audience for a new show, retain that audience, or compete with other broadcasters' programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scheduling strategy (lead-ins, repeats, dayparts) and automation tools are important operational levers for audience-building and competitive positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social, educational, and public-impact considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Television has played a pivotal role in socialization; it can create parasocial relationships, has advantages as an educational tool when used wisely, and is used for religious broadcasting by many denominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing programming, consider potential social impacts (positive educational outcomes versus negative issues like media violence or isolation), target audience needs, and the appropriateness of content for intended social purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product safety and environmental impact considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical television sets pose safety risks (e.g., tip-over injuries especially to young children) and environmental concerns (high lead in CRTs, mercury in lamps for some flat panels), raising issues of electronic waste and occupational health for disassemblers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers, retailers, and policymakers should consider product design (stability), consumer warnings, safe disposal/recycling programs, and material choices to reduce environmental and health harms.
